issues.legal_issue: Accumulated profits from a tea business remain accumulated profits for purposes of taxing a liquidation distribution even when part of those profits was agricultural income exempt from tax in the company’s hands.
material_facts: The companies grew and manufactured tea and accumulated balances in their profit-and-loss accounts and general and taxation reserves.
Under the applicable apportionment rule, 60 per cent of income from tea grown and manufactured by the companies was treated as agricultural income and was not taxable in the companies’ hands.

The companies distributed assets to a shareholder on liquidation, and the dispute concerned whether the agricultural portion of the accumulated balances should be excluded from the amount treated as a dividend.
issues.conclusion: The full amount of the accumulated profit-and-loss balances and reserves distributed to the shareholder was includible as accumulated profits and taxable as a dividend; the agricultural portion was not excluded merely because it had not been taxable in the companies’ hands.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(6A)(c) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, a liquidation distribution is a dividend to the extent attributable to accumulated profits, whether capitalised or not. Rule 24 of the Income-tax Rules, 1922 apportions income from tea grown and manufactured by the seller, but does not require accumulated profits to be apportioned again when distributed. The court would not add the words “as are liable to be taxed under the Act” to section 2(6A)(c). It followed Mrs. Bacha F. Guzdar v. Commissioner of Income-tax, which held that a shareholder’s dividend from a tea company is not agricultural income merely because part of the company’s income was agricultural.

issues.legal_issue: Appreciation in land from which agricultural income is derived is not converted into a capital asset or taxable capital gain by attributing to the land the non-agricultural portion of the income from manufactured tea.
material_facts: The companies owned tea-estate land on which they grew tea, and the land yielded green tea leaves.
The income from selling tea after it was grown and manufactured was integrated income, apportioned between an agricultural component and a manufacturing component.
The companies sold their estates, and the dispute concerned the surplus associated with land and reserves created by revaluing estate assets.
The revenue argued that the portion of tea-sale income treated as non-agricultural made a corresponding proportion of the land a capital asset.
issues.conclusion: The revenue’s proposed proportionate treatment of the land was rejected. The land yielded agricultural income and was excluded from the definition of capital asset, so appreciation in its value did not constitute a capital gain or become a dividend on liquidation; the court upheld the High Court’s treatment of the land and revaluation items.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(4A)(iii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 excludes land from which agricultural income is derived from the definition of capital asset; section 2(6A)(c) addresses liquidation distributions attributable to accumulated profits. Rule 24 apportions the integrated income from tea grown and manufactured by the seller: the agricultural component is derived from the land, while the non-agricultural component is attributable to manufacturing. The court relied on Karimtharuvi Tea Estates Ltd. v. State of Kerala and Anglo-American Direct Tea Trading Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Agricultural Income-tax for the treatment of tea income, and First Income-tax Officer, Salem v. Short Brothers (P.) Ltd. for the treatment of appreciation in agricultural land on liquidation.
